# Trust is part of distribution {#sec-distribution}

A package needs to look trustworthy to the operating system before it can look trustworthy to
a user. Signing connects the package to its publisher and detects later changes.

## Sign the final artifact {#sec-signing}

Deploy first, then sign every contained binary, then sign the installer or disk image. A file
changed after signing loses its signature.

```{mermaid}
flowchart LR
    B[Build] --> T[Test] --> D[Deploy] --> S[Sign application]
    S --> P[Package] --> SP[Sign package] --> N[Notarize on macOS]
```

## macOS needs notarization {#sec-sign-macos}

Outside the App Store, use a Developer ID certificate, the hardened runtime, notarization, and
stapling. Keep the certificate and notarization credentials in the CI secret store, never in
the repository.

Notarization submits the signed app or package to Apple for automated checks. Stapling attaches
the resulting ticket, so Gatekeeper can check it when the user is offline. The template's
release workflow builds packages; it does not configure signing or notarization for you.

## Windows uses Authenticode {#sec-sign-windows}

Sign executables and installers with an Authenticode certificate and a timestamp. The timestamp
keeps a signature valid after the certificate expires. Use a hardware-backed or cloud signing
service for CI keys.

## Stores trade control for services {#sec-stores}

A store handles discovery, trust, and updates, but adds its own sandbox, review process, and
package rules. Choose it when those services are worth the platform constraints.

::: {.more}
**Read more:** [Qt macOS deployment](https://doc.qt.io/qt-6/macos-deployment.html) and
[Microsoft code signing](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/windows/apps/package-and-deploy/code-signing-options).
:::
